title: Cap. 7 Contra open: Obj. 1 — mercy vs justice in elect application
latin:
Contra haec omnia quae disputavimus de speciali intentione Christi morientis relata & restricta ad electos, & de salutifera applicatione mortis Christi ab eadem intentione dependente & dimanante, objici possunt.

1. Si in oblatione Christi detur talis intentio ad electos limitata, unde pro illis obtineatur efficacitas applicationis, & infallibilitas salutis, tum videmur illorum justificationem & salutem non tam ad eudokian, & specialem Dei misericordiam, quam ad rationem quandam justitiae revocare. Nam si quaeratur cur Petrus potius quam Judas gratiam efficacem & salutem ex merito mortis Christi acceperit, juxta nostram sententiam respondendum erit, Quia Christus speciali intentione & applicatione meritorum suorum id nomine Petri promeruit, quod pro Juda mereri noluit. Quod autem datur ex meritis Christi peculiariter applicatis huic personae, non videtur dari ex sola misericordia beneplaciti Divini, sed potius ex justitia: quia justum est ut quod Christus hisce aut illis personis promeruit, eisdem specialiter assignetur. Hoc autem videtur contravenire Apostolo, qui gratiam & salutem infallibilem praedestinatorum a pura Dei gratia arcessit.
pass_a_gloss:
Against all these things which we have disputed concerning the special intention of Christ dying, referred and restricted to the elect, and concerning the saving application of Christ's death depending on and flowing from that same intention, objections can be raised.

1. If in Christ's offering such an intention limited to the elect is granted, from which for them the efficacy of application and the infallibility of salvation are obtained, then we seem to recall their justification and salvation not so much to eudokia and God's special mercy as to a certain account of justice. For if it is asked why Peter rather than Judas received efficacious grace and salvation from the merit of Christ's death, according to our opinion it will have to be answered, Because Christ by special intention and application of his merits merited that in Peter's name which he was unwilling to merit for Judas. But what is given from Christ's merits peculiarly applied to this person does not seem to be given from the sole mercy of the Divine good pleasure, but rather from justice: because it is just that what Christ merited for these or those persons be specially assigned to the same. This however seems to run contrary to the Apostle, who fetches the grace and infallible salvation of the predestined from the pure grace of God.
pass_b:
Against all we have argued about Christ's special dying intention toward the elect, and about the saving application of his death that hangs on and flows from that intention, objections can be raised.

1. If Christ's offering carries an intention limited to the elect, and from it they receive efficacious application and sure salvation, then we seem to ground their justification and salvation less in God's eudokia and special mercy than in a kind of justice. Ask why Peter rather than Judas received efficacious grace and salvation from Christ's death, and on our view the answer must be: because by special intention and application of his merits Christ merited for Peter what he refused to merit for Judas. Yet what comes from Christ's merits peculiarly applied to one person seems to come not from bare mercy of Divine good pleasure, but from justice — for it is just that what Christ merited for these or those persons be specially assigned to them. That seems to clash with the Apostle, who traces the grace and sure salvation of the predestined to God's pure grace alone.

title: Cap. 7 Contra Sol. 1: mercy fulfilled through Christ's merits
latin: Nulla pugna est inter haec duo pronunciata, Deus justificat & salvat Petrum ex pura gratia sive mera sua eudokia, & Deus justificat & salvat Petrum intuens merita Christi pro Petri salute specialiter ordinata & acceptata. Ratio hujus rei in promptu est; nempe, Quod ipse Deus, qui ex mero suo beneplacito & pura misericordia decrevit dare Petro fidem & salutem, decrevit simul non aliter illi haec dare quam per & propter merita Christi Petro singulari quadam ratione destinata & donata, idque ex eadem eudokia & pura misericordia. Quae Dei eudokia opponitur meritis nostris; sed per merita Christi nobis applicata impletur, non evacuatur. Unde Apostolus Heb. xiii. 21. dicit ipsum Deum efficere in nobis beneplacitum suum per Jesum Christum. Quamvis igitur sit mera Dei eudokia, quod Deus velit Petrum efficaci gratia donare & salvare, tamen hujus beneplaciti executio non aliter fit quam per merita Christi. Huc igitur redit summa responsionis nostrae; Quamvis omne opus specialis gratiae quod fit in electis, fiat propter merita Christi specialiter illis applicata, tamen in illorum justificatione & salute veram rationem misericordiae, non justitiae conspici, quia Christus cum meritis suis, cum hoc ipso modo merendi, & offerendi sua merita speciali quodam intuitu habito ad electos, totum, inquam, hoc ex gratuita Dei erga illos voluntate duxit originem.
pass_a_gloss: There is no fight between these two pronouncements: God justifies and saves Peter from pure grace or his mere eudokia, and God justifies and saves Peter looking upon Christ's merits specially ordained and accepted for Peter's salvation. The reason of this matter is ready to hand; namely, That God himself, who from his mere good pleasure and pure mercy decreed to give Peter faith and salvation, decreed at the same time not to give these things to him otherwise than through and on account of Christ's merits destined and given to Peter by a certain singular reason, and that from the same eudokia and pure mercy. Which eudokia of God is opposed to our merits; but through Christ's merits applied to us it is fulfilled, not emptied. Whence the Apostle in Hebrews 13:21 says that God himself works in us his good pleasure through Jesus Christ. Although therefore it is God's mere eudokia that God wills to gift Peter with efficacious grace and to save him, yet the execution of this good pleasure does not happen otherwise than through Christ's merits. To this therefore the sum of our response returns; Although every work of special grace that is done in the elect happens on account of Christ's merits specially applied to them, yet in their justification and salvation the true account of mercy, not of justice, is seen, because Christ with his merits, with this very mode of meriting, and of offering his merits with a certain special regard had toward the elect, drew the whole of this, I say, from God's free will toward them as origin.
pass_b: These two claims do not clash: God justifies and saves Peter by pure grace — his mere eudokia — and God justifies and saves Peter with an eye to Christ's merits specially ordained and accepted for Peter's salvation. The reason is plain. The same God who, from bare good pleasure and pure mercy, decreed faith and salvation for Peter also decreed to give them only through and because of Christ's merits, destined and granted to Peter in a singular way — and that from the same eudokia and pure mercy. God's eudokia stands against our merits; yet through Christ's merits applied to us it is filled out, not voided. So the Apostle says (Hebrews 13:21) that God himself works his good pleasure in us through Jesus Christ. It is therefore mere Divine eudokia that God wills to give Peter efficacious grace and save him; still that good pleasure is carried out only through Christ's merits. Our whole answer comes to this: every work of special grace in the elect is for Christ's merits specially applied to them, yet their justification and salvation show true mercy, not justice — because Christ, with his merits and with this very way of meriting and offering them under a special regard for the elect, drew the whole plan from God's free will toward them.

lemmas.gloss: looking upon / having regard to Christ's merits

title: Cap. 7 Contra Obj. 2: merits applied before faith?
latin: Si ponamus electos obtinere gratiam efficacem, sive fidem salutiferam, exinde quod mors meritumque Christi in cruce patientis speciali quadam intentione illis applicabatur, tum videmur admittere merita passionis Christi quibusdam hominibus imputata sive applicata ante fidem ipsorum: At hoc receptae Theologorum sententiae adversatur, quae ponit fidem esse instrumentum sive medium, sine quo merita passionis Christi singularibus personis non applicantur: Necesse est igitur ut is actu fidelis exstet, qui Christi merita habeat sibi singulariter applicata aut imputata. Quomodo igitur defendi potest specialis haec applicatio meritorum Christi ad electos, nondum factos fideles & credentes?
pass_a_gloss: If we posit that the elect obtain efficacious grace, or saving faith, from the fact that the death and merit of Christ suffering on the cross was being applied to them by a certain special intention, then we seem to admit the merits of Christ's passion imputed or applied to certain human beings before their faith: But this stands against the received opinion of the theologians, which posits that faith is the instrument or medium without which the merits of Christ's passion are not applied to singular persons: It is necessary therefore that he stand actually faithful who has Christ's merits singularly applied or imputed to himself. How then can this special application of Christ's merits to the elect, not yet made faithful and believing, be defended?
pass_b: Suppose the elect gain efficacious grace — saving faith — because Christ's death and merit on the cross were applied to them by a special intention. Then we seem to allow the merits of his passion to be imputed or applied to some people before they believe. That clashes with the received theological rule that faith is the instrument or means without which Christ's passion-merits are not applied to particular persons. So whoever has Christ's merits singularly applied or imputed must already stand as a believer. How then can we defend this special application of Christ's merits to the elect before they are made faithful and believing?

title: Cap. 7 Contra Sol. 2: God-side application; Scotus on joining the unjoined
latin: Ut huic objectioni occurratur, fundamenti loco ponendum est illud Apostoli, Ephes. i. 3. Benedixit nobis Deus omni benedictione spirituali in Christo. Id est, Quicquid boni salutiferi ad nos a Deo descendit, id nobis per Christum & propter merita Christi donatur. Cum igitur ipsa fides salutifera, quae propria est electorum, sit inter praecipuas spirituales benedictiones reponenda, propter merita Christi illam donari iis omnibus, quibus de facto donatur, in confesso est. Quod igitur vulgo dicunt Theologi, fidem esse illud instrumentum, quo mediante merita Christi nobis applicantur, id intelligendum est de applicatione ex parte hominum considerata: Ipsi enim electi non possunt sibi applicare merita Christi ad perceptionem beneficiorum quorumcunque spiritualium, nisi fide in iis praesupposita. At si applicationem aut imputationem ex parte solius Dei consideremus, tum dicendum est, Deum & posse & solere applicare, id est, imputare & communicare, hominibus merita Christi, ita ut intuitu horum meritorum det illis bona spiritualia, etiam cum impii & infideles censeantur. Fides enim ipsa, cum primum datur, non fideli datur, sed infideli: datur autem electis propter merita Mediatoris. Necesse est ergo ut fateamur, neminem ex electis potuisse credendo sibi applicare merita Christi ad fructum vitae aeternae, nisi Deus ex speciali misericordia, propter hoc meritum Christi, fidem qua crederent illis prius infudisset. Atque haec est illa specialis applicatio meritorum Christi quam ex speciali voluntate Christi seipsum offerentis, Deique Patris hoc sacrificium acceptantis, ad electos peculiari quodam privilegio pertinere affirmamus. Scotus huc respexit, illo dicto observatione dignissimo, Haec fuit potissimum in merito Christi, quod meruit non-conjunctos conjungi, lib. 3. dist. 19. qu. unica, pag. 75. Quod perinde est ac si dixisset, praecipuam efficaciam meritorum Christi in eo sitam, quod meruit ut quidam ex infidelibus reapse fierent fideles, Christoque per fidem conjuncti vitam aeternam consequerentur. Haec est illa specialis ordinatio meritorum Christi, atque applicatio, quae tota pendet ex Dei beneplacito, non ex hominum arbitrio.
pass_a_gloss: That this objection may be met, that saying of the Apostle is to be set as a foundation, Ephesians 1:3: God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ. That is, Whatever saving good descends to us from God is gifted to us through Christ and on account of Christ's merits. Since therefore saving faith itself, which is proper to the elect, is to be placed among the chief spiritual blessings, it is confessed that it is gifted on account of Christ's merits to all those to whom it is in fact gifted. What therefore the theologians commonly say, that faith is that instrument by means of which Christ's merits are applied to us, is to be understood of application considered from the side of human beings: For the elect themselves cannot apply Christ's merits to themselves for the perception of any spiritual benefits whatsoever, unless faith is presupposed in them. But if we consider application or imputation from the side of God alone, then it must be said that God both can and is accustomed to apply, that is, to impute and communicate, Christ's merits to human beings, so that with regard to these merits he gives them spiritual goods, even when they are counted as impious and unbelieving. For faith itself, when it is first given, is not given to a believer, but to an unbeliever: yet it is given to the elect on account of the Mediator's merits. It is necessary therefore that we confess that no one of the elect could by believing apply Christ's merits to himself for the fruit of eternal life, unless God from special mercy, on account of this merit of Christ, had first infused into them the faith by which they would believe. And this is that special application of Christ's merits which, from the special will of Christ offering himself, and of God the Father accepting this sacrifice, we affirm pertains to the elect by a certain peculiar privilege. Scotus looked to this in that saying most worthy of observation: This was chiefly in Christ's merit, that he merited that the unjoined be joined, book 3, distinction 19, unique question, page 75. Which is as if he had said that the chief efficacy of Christ's merits is situated in this, that he merited that certain ones from among unbelievers should in fact become faithful, and joined to Christ by faith should obtain eternal life. This is that special ordination of Christ's merits, and application, which wholly depends on God's good pleasure, not on human choice.
pass_b: To meet the objection, take Ephesians 1:3 as foundation: God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ — that is, every saving good that comes down from God is given through Christ and for his merits. Saving faith, proper to the elect, ranks among the chief spiritual blessings; so it is granted, for Christ's merits, to all who in fact receive it. When theologians say faith is the instrument by which Christ's merits are applied to us, they mean application on the human side: the elect cannot apply those merits to themselves for any spiritual benefit unless faith is already presupposed in them. But if we view application or imputation from God's side alone, God can and does apply — impute and communicate — Christ's merits to people so that, with regard to those merits, he gives spiritual goods even while they still count as ungodly and unbelieving. Faith, when first given, is not given to a believer but to an unbeliever; yet it is given to the elect for the Mediator's merits. So we must confess: no elect person could, by believing, apply Christ's merits to himself for eternal life's fruit unless God, from special mercy and for that merit of Christ, had first infused the faith by which they would believe. That is the special application of Christ's merits which, from Christ's special will in offering himself and the Father's in accepting the sacrifice, we say belongs to the elect by a peculiar privilege. Scotus saw this in a saying worth marking: the chief thing in Christ's merit was that he merited the joining of the unjoined (lib. 3, dist. 19, unique q., p. 75) — as if to say the main force of those merits is that some from among unbelievers should become believers and, joined to Christ by faith, obtain eternal life. That special ordination and application of Christ's merits hangs wholly on God's good pleasure, not on human choice.

title: Cap. 7 Contra Obj. 3 + Sol.: OT elects and meritorious cause
latin:
Obj. 3. Si in Christo seipsum offerente, Deoque illud sacrificium acceptante, sit specialis quaedam intentio de vivificandis & infallibiliter salvandis electis omnibus virtute & merito ejusdem sacrificii, videmur ab hoc speciali privilegio excludere electos sub Veteri Testamento, qui nati ac denati fuerunt ante hoc sacrificium Christi in cruce exhibitum.

Sol. Quoad rationem sufficientiae generalis sive efficaciae specialis, respondeo, Christi sacrificium eandem virtutem habuisse sub Veteri Testamento, ante externum actum exhibitionis, quam habuit & habet sub Novo, post Christum realiter in cruce exhibitum & oblatum. Sicuti igitur ad electos sub N. T. ex speciali intentione Dei derivatur gratia specialis a merito hujus sacrificii jam actu exhibiti, ita ad electos sub V. T. ex speciali ejusdem Dei voluntate dimanavit gratia specialis a merito ejusdem sacrificii postmodum exhibendi. Christus enim erat Agnus occisus ab origine mundi, tam in praeparatione voluntatis suae, quam in acceptatione voluntatis Paternae. Est itaque hic observandum, aliam esse rationem causae ejus quae operatur Physice sive naturaliter, aliam ejus quae operatur meritorie sive moraliter. Causa physice agens, actu ponatur est necesse, priusquam ejus virtute effectum aliquod producatur: at causa agens meritorie sive moraliter, qualis est passio Christi, potest effectum producere priusquam actu exsistat, si praecedat saltem in ejus cognitione & acceptatione ad quem spectat ejusdem intuitu beneficia gratiae suae hominibus dispensare. Nam hac in re causa Meritoria habet cognationem quandam cum causa Finali, quae nondum actu exsistens, sed tantummodo praevisa & praeconsiderata, valide movet agentem ad hoc vel illud agendum. Hoc modo dicimus passionem Christi, meritaque ab eadem dependentia, praevisa ut Deo offerenda & applicanda specialiter Jacobo, & non Esavo, habuisse rationem causae moventis Deum ad donandum Jacobo illam specialem gratiam, quam Esavo negavit. Recte Suarez, in 3. qu. 49. art. 4. in comm. Illa specialis dilectio, qua propter merita Christi, sive exhibita sive praevisa, Deus homines sanctificat, & sibi reconciliat, potest cadere sub meritis Christi, sive promerendo nobis effectum illius dilectionis, sive dilectionem (vel electionem) Dei ad nos libere terminatam.
pass_a_gloss:
Obj. 3. If in Christ offering himself, and in God accepting that sacrifice, there is a certain special intention concerning vivifying and infallibly saving all the elect by the virtue and merit of the same sacrifice, we seem to exclude from this special privilege the elect under the Old Testament, who were born and died before this sacrifice of Christ exhibited on the cross.

Sol. As to the account of general sufficiency or of special efficacy, I answer that Christ's sacrifice had the same virtue under the Old Testament, before the external act of exhibition, which it had and has under the New, after Christ was really exhibited and offered on the cross. Just as therefore to the elect under the N.T. special grace is derived from the special intention of God from the merit of this sacrifice already actually exhibited, so to the elect under the O.T. special grace flowed from the special will of the same God from the merit of the same sacrifice afterward to be exhibited. For Christ was the Lamb slain from the origin of the world, both in the preparation of his will and in the acceptance of the Father's will. And so it is to be observed here that there is one account of that cause which operates Physically or naturally, another of that which operates meritoriously or morally. A cause acting physically must be actually posited before some effect is produced by its virtue: but a cause acting meritoriously or morally, such as Christ's passion, can produce an effect before it actually exists, if it at least precedes in the cognition and acceptance of him to whom it pertains to dispense the benefits of his grace to human beings with regard to the same. For in this matter a Meritorious cause has a certain kinship with a Final cause, which, not yet actually existing, but only foreseen and foreconsidered, validly moves the agent to doing this or that. In this way we say that Christ's passion, and the merits depending on the same, foreseen as to be offered to God and applied specially to Jacob and not to Esau, had the account of a moving cause of God to gifting Jacob that special grace which he denied to Esau. Rightly Suarez, in 3, question 49, article 4, in the commentary: That special love by which, on account of Christ's merits, whether exhibited or foreseen, God sanctifies human beings and reconciles them to himself, can fall under Christ's merits, whether by meriting for us the effect of that love, or the love (or election) of God freely terminated toward us.
pass_b:
Obj. 3. If Christ in offering himself, and God in accepting that sacrifice, had a special intention to vivify and surely save all the elect by that sacrifice's virtue and merit, we seem to shut Old Testament elect out of the privilege — those born and dead before Christ's sacrifice was shown on the cross.

Sol. On general sufficiency or special efficacy I answer: Christ's sacrifice had the same virtue under the Old Testament, before the outward act of exhibition, that it has under the New after Christ was really shown and offered on the cross. Just as special grace reaches New Testament elect from God's special intention by the merit of this sacrifice already actually exhibited, so special grace flowed to Old Testament elect from the same God's special will by the merit of that same sacrifice still to be exhibited. For Christ was the Lamb slain from the world's beginning, both in the readiness of his will and in the Father's acceptance. Note the difference: a cause that works physically or naturally must already be in act before its power yields an effect; a cause that works meritoriously or morally — such as Christ's passion — can yield an effect before it actually exists, if it at least stands beforehand in the knowledge and acceptance of him who, with regard to it, dispenses the benefits of his grace. Here a meritorious cause is kin to a final cause: not yet existing in act, but only foreseen and weighed, it still moves the agent to act. So we say Christ's passion and its dependent merits, foreseen as to be offered to God and applied specially to Jacob, not Esau, moved God to give Jacob the special grace he denied Esau. Suarez puts it well (In 3, q. 49, art. 4, comm.): that special love by which, for Christ's merits — exhibited or foreseen — God sanctifies and reconciles people can fall under Christ's merits, whether by meriting for us the effect of that love, or God's love (or election) freely fixed on us.

lemmas.gloss: Lamb slain from the foundation of the world

title: Cap. 7 Contra Obj. 4: incongruity of faith given only to elect
latin: Obj. 4. Ultimo in loco & illud objici potest, Parum consentaneum, imo plane incongruum esse, ut Deus, qui Christi mortem, cum divite thesauro meritorum eodem incluso, omnibus voluerit esse ex aequo sub Fidei conditione applicabilem ad consecutionem vitae aeternae, noluerit interim ex aequo hanc ipsam fidem propter eadem Christi merita omnibus praeparare & donare, sed ipsam fidem perseverantem & salutiferam solis electis dederit, idque propter Christi merita speciali quadam Dei intentione, speciali quodam intuitu ad eos restricta & ordinata.
pass_a_gloss: Obj. 4. Last in place this also can be objected: that it is little fitting, indeed plainly incongruous, that God, who willed Christ's death, with the rich treasury of merits included in the same, to be for all equally applicable under the condition of Faith unto the obtaining of eternal life, should meanwhile have been unwilling equally to prepare and gift this very faith on account of the same merits of Christ to all, but should have given persevering and saving faith itself to the elect alone, and that on account of Christ's merits by a certain special intention of God, by a certain special regard restricted and ordained toward them.
pass_b: Obj. 4. Last comes this charge: it is hardly fitting — indeed plainly incongruous — that God, who willed Christ's death, with its rich treasury of merits, to be equally applicable to all under the condition of faith for obtaining eternal life, should meanwhile refuse to prepare and give that same faith, for those same merits, equally to all, and should give persevering saving faith to the elect alone — and that for Christ's merits by a special Divine intention, a special regard restricted and ordained toward them.

title: Cap. 7 Contra Sol. 4: three reasons; Rupertus and Ambrose
latin: Respondeo, ubi de facto aliquo Divino constat, temerarium est (ne dicam impium) de aequitate aut congruitate ejusdem dubitare. Jam vero Christi morte esse stabilitum illud pactum cum humano genere, ex cujus tenore vita aeterna cuivis homini sub Fidei conditione promittitur, jam pridem a nobis demonstratum est. De hoc pacto Rupertus, in 4. Genes. cap. 34, Dicimus pactum multoties quidem promissum, sed semel initum, quo solo inimicitiae solvuntur, quae erant inter Deum & homines, passio scilicet Christi Filii Dei. Illic enim absque ulla contradictione certa est constitutio pacis, dum accepta Deus Fide hominum dat hominibus eundem Christum Filium suum, ut salventur per ipsum. De hac itaque Dei ordinatione in Christi morte meritisque fundata, atque ad omnes & singulos spectante, non est ambigendum. Verum illud adhuc in dubium vocatur, utrum posito hoc universali pacto dandae vitae aeternae omnibus, si crediderint, Deus exerceat libertatem, & exserat specialem misericordiam in danda hac Fide salutifera electis qua credant; idque per Christum, & propter merita Christi peculiari quodam privilegio ad eos applicata. Res ipsa loquitur. Videmus enim electos, & solos electos, in eventu obtinere a Deo fidem perseverantem & salutiferam: Putare autem tantum ac tale donum illis specialiter donatum alio modo, aut intuitu quam propter merita Christi illis speciali quadam intentione Dei ordinata & applicata, plane nefas est. Nam, ut pie Ambrosius, Omne donum gratiae in Christo est, ad illud Apostoli, Ephes. i. 3. Benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in Christo. Hisce constitutis, quamvis (ut dixi) supervacaneum est de congruitate Divinorum factorum disceptare ubi de ipsis factis constat, tamen, ne quid scrupuli relinquatur, primo dicimus, Hanc specialem Dei intentionem, juxta quam apud se decrevit propter merita Christi dare electis specialia beneficia gratiae efficacis & salutis, non pugnare cum pacto illo conditionato, Quisquis crediderit salvus erit, sed potius esse speciale quoddam consilium, ad universalis hujus pacti infallibilem impletionem subordinatum. Qui enim suo arbitrio committuntur sub quibusvis gratiae adminiculis, aut Fidem repellunt, aut excutiunt. Ne itaque pactum illud universale nemini effectum salutis apportaret, Deus speciali hac & arcana sua intentione curavit aliquibus applicatum iri mortis Christi meritum, ad Fidei vitaeque aeternae infallibilem consecutionem. Secundo, dicimus, Nihil iniqui aut incongrui esse, quod haec specialis intentio de efficaci applicatione meritorum Christi in aliquibus, non in omnibus vim suam exserat; quia cum mors Christi sit gratuitum Dei donum humano generi impensum, libera distributio & applicatio meritorum inde redundantium omni jure ex mera Dei voluntate dependere debeat. Tertio, & illud addimus, Deum, qui in Evangelio promisit omnibus & singulis vitam aeternam propter merita Christi, si crediderint, nulli tamen infidelium promisisse se illi propter merita Christi daturum ut infallibiliter & perseveranter credat. Quaero igitur, Ex qua parte versatur haec incongruitas? Non ex parte credentium & servatorum: Nam dare propter merita Christi singularibus personis quod illis singulariter minime promissum fuit, non est culpandae iniquitatis, sed celebrandae bonitatis. Non ex parte incredulorum & perditorum: Nam illud beneficium negare alicui, quod constat te nulla ratione illi debere, nec in se iniquum, nec summae bonitati Divinae incongruum judicari potest.
pass_a_gloss: I answer: where some Divine fact is established, it is rash (not to say impious) to doubt concerning the equity or fittingness of the same. Now that by Christ's death that pact with the human race has been established, from whose tenor eternal life is promised to any human being under the condition of Faith, has long since been demonstrated by us. Concerning this pact Rupertus, in Genesis book 4, chapter 34: We say a pact many times indeed promised, but once entered, by which alone the enmities which were between God and human beings are loosed, namely the passion of Christ the Son of God. For there without any contradiction the constitution of peace is certain, while God, faith of human beings having been accepted, gives to human beings the same Christ his Son, that they may be saved through him. Concerning this ordination of God therefore, founded in Christ's death and merits, and looking to all and each, there is not to be ambiguity. But that is still called into doubt, whether, this universal pact of giving eternal life to all if they have believed having been posited, God exercises liberty and puts forth special mercy in giving this saving Faith to the elect by which they believe; and that through Christ, and on account of Christ's merits applied to them by a certain peculiar privilege. The matter itself speaks. For we see the elect, and the elect alone, in the event obtain from God persevering and saving faith: But to think so great and such a gift specially gifted to them in another way, or with another regard, than on account of Christ's merits ordained and applied to them by a certain special intention of God, is plainly unlawful. For, as Ambrose piously says, Every gift of grace is in Christ, at that saying of the Apostle, Ephesians 1:3: He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ. These things having been established, although (as I said) it is superfluous to dispute about the fittingness of Divine deeds where the deeds themselves are established, yet, lest any scruple be left, first we say that this special intention of God, according to which he decreed with himself on account of Christ's merits to give the elect the special benefits of efficacious grace and salvation, does not fight with that conditioned pact, Whoever has believed will be saved, but rather is a certain special counsel subordinated to the infallible fulfillment of this universal pact. For those who are committed to their own choice under whatever helps of grace either repel Faith or shake it off. Lest therefore that universal pact should bring the effect of salvation to no one, God by this special and secret intention of his cared that the merit of Christ's death should be applied to some, unto the infallible obtaining of Faith and eternal life. Second, we say that there is nothing unjust or incongruous in that this special intention concerning the efficacious application of Christ's merits puts forth its force in some, not in all; because since Christ's death is a free gift of God expended on the human race, the free distribution and application of the merits overflowing thence ought by every right to depend on the mere will of God. Third, we also add that God, who in the Gospel promised to all and each eternal life on account of Christ's merits if they have believed, yet promised to none of the unbelieving that he would give to him on account of Christ's merits that he should believe infallibly and perseveringly. I ask therefore, From which side does this incongruity turn? Not from the side of believers and the saved: For to give on account of Christ's merits to singular persons what was least singularly promised to them is not of blameworthy injustice, but of goodness to be celebrated. Not from the side of the unbelieving and the lost: For to deny to someone that benefit which it is established you owe him by no account can be judged neither unjust in itself nor incongruous with the highest Divine goodness.
pass_b: I answer: once a Divine fact stands, it is rash — not to say impious — to quarrel with its equity or fittingness. We have long shown that by Christ's death that covenant with the human race was fixed, by whose terms eternal life is promised to anyone under the condition of faith. On that covenant Rupert of Deutz (on Genesis 4.34) says: we call it a covenant many times promised but once struck, by which alone the enmities between God and humankind are dissolved — namely the passion of Christ the Son of God. There peace is settled without contradiction when God, receiving human faith, gives people the same Christ his Son that they may be saved through him. So there is no doubt about this Divine ordination, founded in Christ's death and merits and looking to every person. What is still doubted is whether, given this universal covenant of eternal life for all who believe, God may freely show special mercy in giving the elect the saving faith by which they believe — and that through Christ, for his merits applied to them by a peculiar privilege. The fact itself speaks. We see the elect alone, in the outcome, receive from God persevering saving faith. To imagine so great a gift given them in any other way or regard than for Christ's merits, ordained and applied by a special Divine intention, is plainly unlawful. As Ambrose says devoutly, every gift of grace is in Christ — pointing to Ephesians 1:3, He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ. That settled, though it is needless to debate the fittingness of Divine deeds when the deeds themselves are clear, still, to leave no scruple: first, this special intention by which God decreed, for Christ's merits, to give the elect the special benefits of efficacious grace and salvation does not fight the conditioned covenant Whoever believes will be saved; it is rather a special counsel subordinated to that universal covenant's sure fulfillment. Those left to their own choice under any helps of grace either push faith away or shake it off. Lest that universal covenant bring salvation's effect to no one, God by this special and secret intention saw to it that Christ's death-merit would be applied to some for the sure obtaining of faith and eternal life. Second, nothing unjust or incongruous follows if this special intention of efficacious application of Christ's merits puts forth its force in some, not in all: Christ's death is God's free gift to the human race, so free distribution and application of the overflowing merits ought by every right to hang on God's mere will. Third, God, who in the Gospel promised every person eternal life for Christ's merits if they believe, never promised any unbeliever that for those merits he would make him believe surely and perseveringly. So where is the incongruity? Not on the side of believers and the saved: to give singular persons, for Christ's merits, what was never singularly promised them is not blameworthy injustice but goodness to praise. Not on the side of the unbelieving and lost: to deny someone a benefit you owe him by no title is neither unjust in itself nor unfit for God's highest goodness.

title: Cap. 7 close: sufficient for all, efficacious for elect — Amen
latin: Sit itaque haec totius hujus controversiae De Morte Christi summa & conclusio; Mediatorem Dei ac hominum, Jesum Christum, in foedere illo Evangelico sanciendo, ex cujus tenore omni credenti debetur vita aeterna, nullam partitionem hominum vel discretionem instituisse, ut quenquam dicere possimus a mortis suae beneficio exclusum, si crederet: Atque hoc sensu, suffragantibus Scripturis, Patribus, ac solidis rationibus, tuemur, Christum pro omnibus hominibus, sive pro toto humano genere, in cruce passum ac mortuum fuisse. Quinetiam addimus & hoc, Eundem Mediatorem, cum animam suam pro peccato decrevisset ponere, habuisse insuper hanc singularem intentionem, quod virtute meritorum suorum efficaciter & infallibiliter quosdam sibi a Patre singulariter datos esset vivificaturus & ad vitam perducturus: Atque hoc sensu defendimus, Christum pro solis Electis, vel pro Ecclesia sua acquirenda, animam suam posuisse, id est, pro illis solis mortuum fuisse cum hoc singulari & certo proposito per meritum mortis suae eos efficaciter regenerandi & salvandi. Quamvis ergo meritum Christi aequaliter se habeat ad omnes quoad sufficientiam, non tamen quoad efficaciam: quod intelligendum est non tantum ex parte effectus, qui in uno fit & non in alio, sed etiam ex parte voluntatis, qua ipse Christus meruit, & diverso modo obtulit sua merita pro diversis. Prima autem radix hujus diversitatis fuit electio & voluntas Divina, cui se voluntas humana Christi conformavit. Atque hinc recte deducit Suarez, Meritum hoc Christi esse causam ipsius spiritualis regenerationis, & dare illi efficaciam, & influere in effectum ejus, & simul causam esse ut hic homo regeneretur, propter quem specialiter suum obtulit meritum, In 3. qu. 19. disp. 41. S. 2. pag. 635. Pro nostris loquatur vir eximiae eruditionis & piae memoriae Robertus Sarisburiensis; sic igitur ille, in Thomson. Diatrib. pag. 94. Nos etsi Christum pro omnibus mortuum non negamus, specialiter tamen & proprie credimus mortuum esse pro Ecclesia, neque ad omnes homines beneficium redemtionis pari jure pertinere. Atque ab hujus beneficii proprietate, non ab humana aliquatenus voluntate pendet efficacia mediorum omnium, ut illis tantum sint, & ex usu sint, quos Christus in se electos peculiari quodam intuitu redemit: neque ex eo effectum sortiantur, quia nos volumus, sed ex eo quod in electis & redemtis secundum propositum gratiae suae operatur Deus hoc velle ad quod elegit. Qui igitur morte sua omnibus sufficientissime promeruit vitam aeternam, donandam utique omnibus ex pacto Evangelico, si crederent; is aliquibus ex peculiari meritorum suorum applicatione promeruit efficacissime ut crederent, ut vitam aeternam ex gratuito Dei dono per & propter Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum acciperent. Atque haec est sors electorum peculiaris: Cujus nos omnes participes faciat Pater misericordiarum, cui cum Filio & Spiritu Sancto sit honor, laus & gloria nunc & in secula sempiterna. Amen.
pass_a_gloss: Let this therefore be the sum and conclusion of this whole controversy On the Death of Christ; that the Mediator of God and human beings, Jesus Christ, in establishing that Evangelical covenant, from whose tenor eternal life is owed to every believer, instituted no partition of human beings or discrimination, so that we could say anyone was excluded from the benefit of his death, if he believed: And in this sense, with the Scriptures, Fathers, and solid reasons assenting, we maintain that Christ suffered and died on the cross for all human beings, or for the whole human race. Moreover we also add this, that the same Mediator, when he had decreed to lay down his soul for sin, had besides this singular intention, that by the virtue of his merits he would efficaciously and infallibly vivify and lead to life certain ones singularly given to him by the Father: And in this sense we defend that Christ laid down his soul for the Elect alone, or for acquiring his Church, that is, that he died for them alone with this singular and certain purpose of efficaciously regenerating and saving them through the merit of his death. Although therefore Christ's merit holds itself equally toward all as to sufficiency, yet not as to efficacy: which is to be understood not only from the side of the effect, which happens in one and not in another, but also from the side of the will by which Christ himself merited, and in a diverse manner offered his merits for diverse persons. But the first root of this diversity was Divine election and will, to which Christ's human will conformed itself. And from this Suarez rightly deduces that this merit of Christ is the cause of spiritual regeneration itself, and gives it efficacy, and influences into its effect, and at the same time is the cause that this human being is regenerated, for whom he specially offered his merit, In 3, question 19, disputation 41, section 2, page 635. Let a man of outstanding learning and pious memory, Robert of Salisbury, speak for ours; thus therefore he, in Thomson's Diatribe, page 94: Although we do not deny that Christ died for all, yet we specially and properly believe that he died for the Church, and that the benefit of redemption does not pertain to all human beings by equal right. And on the peculiarity of this benefit, not on the human will to any degree, hangs the efficacy of all the means, so that they are and are of use only for those whom Christ redeemed in himself as elect by a certain peculiar regard: nor do they obtain effect from this, because we will, but from this, that in the elect and redeemed according to the purpose of his grace God works this willing for which he elected. He therefore who by his death most sufficiently merited eternal life for all, to be gifted indeed to all from the Evangelical pact if they believed; he for some by a peculiar application of his merits most efficaciously merited that they should believe, that they should receive eternal life from God's free gift through and on account of our Lord Jesus Christ. And this is the peculiar lot of the elect: Of which may the Father of mercies make us all partakers, to whom with the Son and the Holy Spirit be honor, praise, and glory now and unto everlasting ages. Amen.
pass_b: Let this be the sum and close of the whole controversy On the Death of Christ. The Mediator between God and humankind, Jesus Christ, in sealing that evangelical covenant by which eternal life is due to every believer, made no partition or sorting of people by which we could say anyone was shut out from the benefit of his death if he believed. In that sense — with Scripture, the Fathers, and solid reasons agreeing — we hold that Christ suffered and died on the cross for all human beings, for the whole human race. We add this too: the same Mediator, when he decreed to lay down his life for sin, also had this singular intention — that by the virtue of his merits he would efficaciously and surely vivify and bring to life certain ones singularly given him by the Father. In that sense we defend that Christ laid down his life for the elect alone, or to acquire his Church — that is, he died for them alone with this singular, fixed purpose of efficaciously regenerating and saving them through the merit of his death. So Christ's merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, yet not as to efficacy — and that not only from the effect, which lands in one and not another, but from the will by which Christ himself merited and offered his merits in different ways for different people. The first root of that diversity was Divine election and will, to which Christ's human will conformed. From this Suarez rightly draws that this merit of Christ is the cause of spiritual regeneration itself, gives it efficacy, influences its effect, and is at once the cause that this person is regenerated for whom he specially offered his merit (In 3, q. 19, disp. 41, §2, p. 635). Let Robert of Salisbury, of rare learning and pious memory, speak for our side (in Thomson's Diatribe, p. 94): though we do not deny that Christ died for all, yet we specially and properly believe he died for the Church, and that redemption's benefit does not belong to all by equal right. On that benefit's peculiarity — not on human will — hangs the efficacy of every means, so that they are and are useful only for those whom Christ redeemed in himself as elect under a peculiar regard; nor do they take effect because we will, but because in the elect and redeemed, according to the purpose of his grace, God works the willing for which he chose them. He who by his death most sufficiently merited eternal life for all — to be given to all under the evangelical covenant if they believed — also, by a peculiar application of his merits, most efficaciously merited for some that they should believe and receive eternal life as God's free gift through and for our Lord Jesus Christ. That is the elect's peculiar lot. May the Father of mercies make us all partakers of it; to him, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, be honor, praise, and glory now and forever. Amen.
